description_full: Constellation Energy Corporation produces and sells energy products and services in the United States. The company operates through five segments: Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, New York, ERCOT, and Other Power Regions. It offers electricity, natural gas, energy-related products, and sustainable solutions. The company has approximately 31,676 megawatts of generating capacity consisting of nuclear, wind, solar, natural gas, and hydroelectric assets. It serves distribution utilities, municipalities, cooperatives, and commercial, industrial, public sector, and residential customers. The company was incorporated in 2021 and is headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland.

Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Constellation Energy Corporatio is a large-cap utilities business with a $98.5B market cap on $25.5B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +3.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.83× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.0×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.9%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 201% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Operating margins 9% below sector median — a cost disadvantage the moat cannot hide
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sector_tailwinds: Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 12% operating margin trails the Utilities median (21%) by 9pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+62.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 11% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 50% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.03 vs 5y 1.22), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $824.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 20% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $93.23 (margin of safety -201%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $63.80 to $137 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Utilities peers: P/FCF 76.5 vs 20.0 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $338 on average, 21% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 22.2% annual cash-flow growth, 17pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.81).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.83x.
ROE of 16% is amplified by 3.9x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($3.6B of cash against $9.0B of debt), with interest covered 6.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.5% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 29% of profits supports about 2.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01 and a backlog worth 4% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 11.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Analysts expect 7.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 85%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase, net $418K bought).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.9% (0.4% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
people: With about 15,291 employees, each generates about $1.7M of revenue, 1.6x the Utilities median.
That works out to $84K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.5M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
